claim: AHA can be readily incorporated into the Shaker Kv channel in Xenopus oocytes.
source: Using the Shaker voltage-activated potassium (Kv) channel as a test case, we find that AHA can be readily incorporated into the channel and enables site-specific installation of fluorophores in the protein via a catalyst-independent strain-promoted azide-alkyne cycloaddition (SPAAC) reaction in live Xenopus laevis oocytes (Figure 1B) (Agard et al., 2004).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental results shown in Figure 1E

claim: AHA enables site-specific installation of fluorophores in the Shaker Kv channel via SPAAC reaction in live Xenopus laevis oocytes.
source: Using the Shaker voltage-activated potassium (Kv) channel as a test case, we find that AHA can be readily incorporated into the channel and enables site-specific installation of fluorophores in the protein via a catalyst-independent strain-promoted azide-alkyne cycloaddition (SPAAC) reaction in live Xenopus laevis oocytes (Figure 1B) (Agard et al., 2004).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental results shown in Figures 3 and 4

claim: Fluorophores attached to AHA can be used to track conformational changes of the voltage-sensor in a manner analogous to cysteine-based methods.

evidence: Demonstrated through voltage-clamp fluorometry experiments shown in Figures 3 and 4

claim: AHA incorporation and cysteine mutagenesis can be combined for two-color labeling of membrane proteins in a site-specific manner.

evidence: Demonstrated through experimental results shown in Figures 7 and 8

claim: The Shaker Kv channel contains 12 methionine residues in each subunit.
source: The Shaker Kv channel contains 12 methionine residues in each subunit, 5 of which are in TM regions of the channel (Figure 1C, cyan) (Long et al., 2007).

claim: 5 out of 12 methionine residues in each Shaker Kv channel subunit are in transmembrane regions.
source: The Shaker Kv channel contains 12 methionine residues in each subunit, 5 of which are in TM regions of the channel (Figure 1C, cyan) (Long et al., 2007).

claim: Two out of five methionine residues in the transmembrane regions of Shaker (M356 and M448) face the extracellular side of the channel.

evidence: Supported by citations to previous cysteine accessibility experiments

claim: AHA is typically incorporated into proteins in eukaryotic expression systems by adding the non-canonical amino acid into methionine-free cell culture medium at concentrations ranging from 1 to 4 mM.

claim: AHA-supplemented oocytes showed a single band for the mature Shaker Kv channel subunits in the surface fraction isolated with DBCO-sulfo-biotin.
source: AHA-supplemented oocytes showed a single band for the mature Shaker Kv channel subunits in the surface fraction isolated with DBCO-sulfo-biotin (Figure 1E, surface fraction, lane 2), indicating successful incorporation of AHA into the Shaker Kv channel.
evidence: Shown in western blot data in Figure 1E

claim: No pull-down was observed with DBCO-sulfo-biotin in the absence of AHA.

evidence: Shown in western blot data in Figure 1E

claim: DBCO is chemically selective and does not react with other residues of the protein in the absence of AHA.
source: No pull-down was observed with DBCO-sulfo-biotin in the absence of AHA (Figure 1E, surface fraction, lane 1), although the protein expression was similar in both the cases (Figure 1E, total cell protein, lane 1 and 2), demonstrating that the DBCO is chemically selective and does not react with other residues of the protein.
evidence: Inferred from the absence of pull-down without AHA shown in Figure 1E

claim: Introduction of AHA into the Shaker Kv channel has no detectable effect on expression and trafficking of the channel in Xenopus oocytes.
source: In contrast, pull down with NHS-sulfo-biotin yielded similar amounts of protein both in the absence and presence of AHA (Figure 1E, surface fraction and total cell protein, lane 3 and 4), indicating that introduction of AHA into the Shaker Kv channel has no detectable effect on expression and trafficking of the channel in Xenopus oocytes.

claim: AHA supplementation had no toxic effects on the survival of oocytes in ND96 at 17°C.

claim: AHA specifically replaces methionine residues in membrane proteins expressed in Xenopus oocytes.

claim: The endogenous protein synthesis machinery of Xenopus oocytes can robustly incorporate AHA into newly expressed heterologous proteins.

claim: AHA supplementation does not alter the surface expression of the Shaker Kv channel.

claim: AHA incorporation does not detectably alter the overall process of voltage-dependent gating in the Shaker Kv channel.
source: When the membrane voltage was stepped between −100 mV and +50 mV, we observed robust voltage-activated K+ currents in the presence and absence of AHA, with voltage-activation relationships that were not discernably different (Figure 2A,B), suggesting that AHA incorporation does not detectably alter the overall process of voltage-dependent gating in the Shaker Kv channel.
evidence: Shown in ionic current recordings and G-V relationships in Figure 2A,B

claim: Voltage-sensor activation was not detectably altered with AHA incorporation.

evidence: Shown in gating current recordings and Q-V relationships in Figure 2C,D

claim: GxTx1E toxin produced robust and indistinguishable shifts of voltage-activation relationships to more positive voltages in the absence and presence of AHA.
source: Using a construct of the Shaker Kv channel that is sensitive to the tarantula toxin GxTx1E (ShakerΔ5) (Herrington et al., 2006; Milescu et al., 2009; Milescu et al., 2013), we observed that the toxin produced robust and indistinguishable shifts of voltage-activation relationships to more positive voltages, both in the absence and presence of AHA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown in toxin sensitivity experiments in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Global replacement of methionine residues with AHA in the Shaker Kv channel does not result in detectable alterations in the gating properties of the channel.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that global replacement of methionine residues with AHA in the Shaker Kv channel does not result in detectable alterations in the gating properties of the channel.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from data in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1
